name: ACP-105

card.summary: A discontinued experimental SARM tested in rats and mice; no human trials, sold online as a research chemical.
card.note: Preclinical only; banned in sport; no human safety data.

quick.overview:
ACP-105 is an experimental SARM from the late 2000s. Rodent studies showed muscle-related effects and some cognitive findings.

No human trials were found; it is unapproved.
quick.mechanism: It acts as a partial agonist at the androgen receptor, producing smaller effects than testosterone in tissues tested in rats.
quick.risks: Human safety is unknown. SARMs as a class are banned in sport and have been linked in reports to liver injury and hormone suppression.

lead: ACP-105 is an investigational nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) with partial agonist activity relative to testosterone, described in a 2009 Journal of Medicinal Chemistry paper.[1][2] SARMs were designed to build muscle and bone while acting less on tissues such as the prostate, which is the reason bodybuilders and athletes show interest in them as a route to more muscle mass.[8]

It was discovered through a high-throughput screen using receptor selection and amplification technology, and improved anabolic parameters in castrated male rats.[1] Later animal work examined it in models of age-related cognitive decline and radiation-related deficits.[3][4]

It is not approved for any use. SARMs are banned in sport, and doping-control laboratories have published mass-spectrometric and metabolite studies of ACP-105 in human-sample and equine assays; a 2025 computational study estimated its toxicity profile.[5][6][9][10]

chain: Oral SARM binds the androgen receptor
Partial agonist activity in muscle and bone
angle.text: People who seek ACP-105 as a research chemical hope that selective androgen receptor activation adds lean muscle with fewer androgenic effects. Published work consists of rat and mouse studies, and no human trial exists.

paras: ACP-105 was characterised in 2009 as a partial agonist of the androgen receptor, with the series discovered by screening in a receptor selection and amplification assay and tested for anabolic effect in castrated male rats.[1] Researchers have not settled how SARMs achieve tissue selectivity; proposals include lack of activation by 5-alpha-reductase in the prostate, differences in coregulator proteins between tissues, non-genomic signalling and differences in tissue uptake.[8]
Computational ADME and toxicity work published in 2025 described the compound's predicted absorption, distribution and toxicity, noting that its human safety profile has not been explored.[9][11]

ACP-105 is an aniline-type SARM structurally related to AC-262536 and RAD140 (vosilasarm).[2] Metabolites have been characterised in horse urine after oral administration, in vitro in equine liver preparations and in human in vivo samples, mainly to support doping control.[6][10][12]
The 2009 paper reported synthesis and structure-activity relationships of novel nonsteroidal SARMs and the characterisation of ACP-105 within that series.[1]

In a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, ACP-105 alone and in combination with an estrogen receptor beta agonist was reported to moderate cognitive deficits and amyloid-beta levels; alone it reduced anxiety-like behaviour, and with AC-186 it improved spatial memory.[2][3] A 2011 study examined its effects on rotarod performance and cued fear conditioning in sham-irradiated and irradiated female mice.[4]
No studies found in humans. All published efficacy work is in cells and animals.[1][3][4]

No human safety data were identified for ACP-105. Reviews of the SARM class describe elevated liver enzymes, reduced HDL cholesterol and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in some trials, case reports linking recreational SARM use to liver injury, and unknown cardiovascular risk. SARMs cannot be converted to estrogen, so estrogen-related effects are not expected.[8] The US FDA states that SARMs are unapproved and cannot legally be marketed as supplements or drugs; products sold as research chemicals are often reported to be mislabelled.[8]

SARMs have been prohibited in sport as anabolic agents under World Anti-Doping Agency rules since 2008, and metabolite identification for doping control was reported in 2014.[7][8] Papers describing mass-spectrometric characterisation of RAD140 and ACP-105 (2013) and equine metabolite studies (2021, 2022) were published to extend testing assays.[5][6][10][12]

SARMs are sold on gray markets, often labelled as research chemicals, and are used for muscle growth by bodybuilders and athletes; some jurisdictions treat marketing SARMs for human consumption as illegal, with criminal convictions reported.[8]
